title: Jeremiah 7:16–28
context: The LORD continues speaking to Jeremiah. He forbids him to pray or intercede for the people, because he will not hear (7:16; compare 11:14 and 14:11), and points to whole families making cakes for “the queen of the sky” and pouring out drink offerings to other gods (7:17–18; compare 44:17). The LORD then says that his anger will be poured out on the land (7:20). In 7:21–23 he tells them to add burnt offerings to sacrifices and eat the meat, for in the day he brought their fathers out of Egypt he did not command them about burnt offerings or sacrifices, but commanded, “Listen to my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people.” How to read this statement alongside the sacrificial laws is discussed; many read it as a strong way of putting obedience first (compare 1 Samuel 15:22 and Hosea 6:6), and this page does not press further. The unit closes with the LORD’s summary of a long history of not listening to the prophets and the charge that “Truth has perished” (7:24–28). Both traditions treat the prayer prohibition as shared ground about the seriousness of judgment, while both continue to affirm prayer and intercession generally.

verses.text: “Therefore don’t pray for this people. Don’t lift up a cry or prayer for them or make intercession to me; for I will not hear you.
verses.arminianNotes: “Therefore don’t pray for this people.” Arminian readers hear a solemn sign that judgment is near. They read it as a specific word to Jeremiah in this situation, not a general rule, and they continue to affirm intercession (compare 11:14 and 14:11).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the command as a sign of settled judgment on a people who persist in sin, given to Jeremiah in a particular moment. Shared ground: both traditions affirm prayer and intercession generally and treat this prohibition with sobriety, without drawing a wider rule from it.

verses.text: Don’t you see what they do in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem?
verses.arminianNotes: God asks Jeremiah whether he sees “what they do in the cities of Judah.” Arminian readers note that God points Jeremiah to the visible evidence. The prohibition on prayer is tied to what the people are openly doing, not to an arbitrary decision.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God grounding his word in the people’s public conduct. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as explaining the prohibition by reference to the people’s open idolatry, which the next verse describes.

verses.text: The children gather wood, and the fathers kindle the fire, and the women knead the dough, to make cakes to the queen of the sky, and to pour out drink offerings to other gods, that they may provoke me to anger.
verses.arminianNotes: Children gather wood, fathers kindle the fire, and women knead dough for “the queen of the sky.” Arminian readers note that whole families share in the idolatry. Worship of other gods has become a household practice (compare 44:17).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the spread of idolatry through every part of the family. The identity of the queen of the sky is not stated in the text, and both hold claims about it loosely. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a sober picture of communal unfaithfulness.

verses.text: Do they provoke me to anger?” says the LORD. “Don’t they provoke themselves, to the confusion of their own faces?”
verses.arminianNotes: “Do they provoke me to anger?… Don’t they provoke themselves, to the confusion of their own faces?” Arminian readers note that idolatry harms the idolaters. Their sin brings shame and ruin on themselves.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see that sin against God is also self-destructive. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as teaching that turning from God to idols ends in confusion and shame for those who do it.

verses.text: Therefore the Lord GOD says: “Behold, my anger and my wrath will be poured out on this place, on man, on animal, on the trees of the field, and on the fruit of the ground; and it will burn and will not be quenched.”
verses.arminianNotes: God declares, “my anger and my wrath will be poured out on this place.” Arminian readers note the scope of the judgment, reaching people, animals, trees, and fields. The land shares in the consequences of the people’s sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s just wrath against persistent covenant breaking. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly as an announcement of judgment that will not be quenched, and both see it as the response of a holy God to real evil.

verses.text: The LORD of Armies, the God of Israel says: “Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices and eat meat.
verses.arminianNotes: “Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices and eat meat.” Arminian readers hear irony. Since the people’s offerings are not accepted, they might as well eat the meat themselves, because their sacrifices bring them no favor with God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear a sharp rebuke of sacrifice offered without obedience. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as ironic speech exposing the emptiness of ritual detached from faithfulness, not as a rejection of all worship.

verses.text: For I didn’t speak to your fathers or command them in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt concerning burnt offerings or sacrifices;
verses.arminianNotes: God says he did not command the fathers “concerning burnt offerings or sacrifices” when he brought them out of Egypt. Arminian readers often read this as a strong way of putting obedience first rather than a denial of the sacrificial laws.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the statement as setting priorities, comparing 1 Samuel 15:22 and Hosea 6:6, and hold the precise sense with care. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as stressing that sacrifice was never meant to replace listening to God’s voice.

verses.text: but this thing I commanded them, saying, ‘Listen to my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people. Walk in all the way that I command you, that it may be well with you.’
verses.arminianNotes: “Listen to my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people.” Arminian readers note that the heart of the covenant is relationship and obedience. God’s desire is for a people who walk in his ways.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the covenant formula at the center of God’s purpose for his people. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as summarizing what God wanted from the beginning: a listening, obedient people with whom he dwells as their God.

verses.text: But they didn’t listen or turn their ear, but walked in their own counsels and in the stubbornness of their evil heart, and went backward, and not forward.
verses.arminianNotes: “But they didn’t listen… and went backward, and not forward.” Arminian readers note the tragic direction of the people’s history. Instead of growing in faithfulness, they followed the stubbornness of their own hearts.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the stubbornness of the heart as the root of the people’s failure. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a sober diagnosis of persistent disobedience, and both see the heart as the place where faithfulness or rebellion begins.

verses.text: Since the day that your fathers came out of the land of Egypt to this day, I have sent to you all my servants the prophets, daily rising up early and sending them.
verses.arminianNotes: God sent his servants the prophets “daily rising up early and sending them.” Arminian readers note God’s persistent pursuit. He kept sending messengers, showing his patience and his desire for the people to return.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s faithful provision of the prophetic word throughout Israel’s history. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing God’s long patience and the many opportunities given to the people to listen.

verses.text: Yet they didn’t listen to me or incline their ear, but made their neck stiff. They did worse than their fathers.
verses.arminianNotes: “Yet they didn’t listen… They did worse than their fathers.” Arminian readers note that the people’s refusal grew over time. Each generation had the chance to turn but added to the guilt of the last.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the deepening of sin across generations. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a sober statement of accumulated guilt, and both see in it the seriousness of refusing God’s repeated warnings.

verses.text: “You shall speak all these words to them, but they will not listen to you. You shall also call to them, but they will not answer you.
verses.arminianNotes: “You shall speak all these words to them, but they will not listen to you.” Arminian readers note that Jeremiah is sent even though rejection is expected. His faithfulness is measured by speaking, not by results.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the prophet called to faithful witness regardless of response. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as encouragement for those who speak God’s word without visible success, and neither builds a wider doctrine from it.

verses.text: You shall tell them, ‘This is the nation that has not listened to the LORD their God’s voice, nor received instruction. Truth has perished, and is cut off from their mouth.’
verses.arminianNotes: “Truth has perished, and is cut off from their mouth.” Arminian readers note the summary verdict. A nation that will not listen to God loses truth itself, and its speech becomes empty of faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the loss of truth as the fruit of refusing God’s voice. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a sober conclusion to the unit, describing a people whose refusal to receive instruction has emptied their words of truth.
